title: 2027-06-11 Cascade escalation postmortem follow-up
summary: Follow-up on the May 28th production incident where a KV-cache eviction + autoscaler interaction caused elevated tail latency and a partial degradation for Cascade's Dedicated pool. Discussed root cause, confirmed short-term mitigations, and agreed on medium-term reliability improvements and a shared test plan.
topics: Root cause analysis: KV cache and autoscaler interplay
Short-term mitigations (TTL, cache warming, autoscale thresholds)
Long-term fixes: autoscaler tuning, canary deploys, pre-warm hooks
Security/compliance notes: audit logs and KMS handling
next_steps: Redwood to share narrowed postmortem deck and logs (internal sanitized) by 2027-06-14
Cascade SRE to provide representative workload traces and spike patterns by 2027-06-18
Schedule 48-hour soak test on a replica Dedicated pool w/ pre-warm and adjusted autoscaler (target week of 2027-06-21)
Joint reliability workshop (Ravi + Cascade SREs) to finalize autoscaler policy and KV cache TTL strategy by 2027-06-25
action_items: Ravi Patel (Redwood SE): collect and push sanitized per-request traces and KV-cache hit-rate graphs to shared GDrive - due 2027-06-14
Laura Kim (Redwood AE): send updated pricing for a temporary Dedicated burst pool for soak testing and confirm billing terms - due 2027-06-15
Sofia Ruiz (Cascade SRE): export tpm/p95/p99 traces for the May 28th window and attach example slow queries - due 2027-06-18
Daniel O'Neill (Cascade Security): confirm if audit log retention change requires re-review by compliance - due 2027-06-20
Priya Nair (Cascade EngMgr): provision a staging job to replay the observed traffic pattern and report results - due 2027-06-21
transcript:
Header: 2027-06-11 15:30 UTC | Duration: 52m | Recording: Zoom | Meeting title: Cascade escalation postmortem follow-up
Attendees: Laura Kim (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Janelle Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Markus Li (Cascade Head of Platform), Sofia Ruiz (Cascade SRE), Daniel O'Neill (Cascade Head of Security), Priya Nair (Cascade EngMgr)

Auto-summary: quick recap of May 28th incident, RCA discussed, agreed short and medium term mitigations, set owners and dates for next steps.

[00:00] Laura K: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh i'll kick off. quick agenda - recap the outage, rca, mitigations, next steps.
[00:12] Markus L: thanks laura, appreciate it. we mostly want to be sure this wont repeat and that the mitigation plan is measurable.
[00:20] Ravi P: quick note, we'll try to keep the technical deep dive to 20 min and then go action items. there may be a couple of slides i sent earlier, link in the chat.
[00:35] Sofia R: yes got the slides, though some of the metric names in the deck look slightly different than what our dashboards show - e.g. p99 request vs p99 token latency, small naming mismatch.
[00:50] Laura K: noted, we'll reconcile naming in the final doc. ok rca recap - on May 28 at ~14:23 UTC we observed a sudden spike in tail latency that affected about 18% of requests to your dedicated pool. latency presented as p95 doubling and p99 spike to several seconds, some requests timed out.
[01:12] Priya N: that match our alert timeline. the spike coincided with a batch job on our side that hit a long tail of sequences.
[01:25] Ravi P: yep, our analysis points to a KV-cache eviction storm, triggered by a combination of increased prefix variance and the autoscaler aggressively tearing down warm workers during a perceived idle window. basically cache thrash + cold starts.
[01:42] Markus L: can you explain "kv-cache eviction storm" in plain terms? some of our stakeholders are non-dev.
[01:48] Ravi P: sure - the runtime keeps per-request kv state to avoid recomputing prefixes; when instances scale down quickly, cached kv entries are evicted, so the next set of requests have to rebuild cache which is expensive and increases latency. if many workers are torn down at once you get a storm.
[02:10] Sofia R: we saw memory pressure on the worker VMs right before - curious if memory limits plus the eviction policy played in.
[02:18] Ravi P: very possibly, yes. also interplay with batch size - some kernels are sensitive to sequence length variance which amplifies per-token cost.
[02:30] Janelle O: small interjection - we did fallback to a hosted-compatible variant for a small subset during the incident; that kept error rate lower but cost spiked.
[02:42] Markus L: was that automated?
[02:44] Laura K: yes the smart routing policy triggered fallback to a cheaper hosted model variant for non-sensitive routes; we can disable that if you want to avoid variability.
[02:55] Daniel O: from a security perspective, i want to confirm no data exfil, and that audit logs captured the timeframe. i also want to know about KMS usage during rollbacks.
[03:07] Ravi P: logs are intact; we retained request ids and audit entries. KMS usage was normal - no key rotation or key exposure. we'll include the ILM for audit retention in the deck.
[03:21] Laura K: quick note - transcription may have errors, there were some cross talk moments.
[03:30] [Slide share start - RCA timing chart]
[03:35] Ravi P: timeline - 14:20 small spike in variance, 14:23 p95 starts climbing, 14:25 autoscaler scaled down a group of workers due to a heuristic (short idle period), 14:26 full kv-cache miss waves, 14:28 p99 peaks, 14:34 partial fallback triggered, 14:50 gradual recovery after manual intervention.
[04:05] Sofia R: in the logs we see a lot of cache-miss churn exactly during 14:26-14:32. i'll upload the sample traces.
[04:15] Ravi P: couple of immediate mitigations we rolled out during the incident: 1) temporarily raised min replica count to avoid aggressive teardown, 2) increased KV cache ttl to reduce eviction churn, 3) disabled autoscale down for 10 minutes after high-variance bursts. these were manual and helped stabilize.
[04:40] Markus L: ok did you see any request-level errors, or was it primarily timeouts/latency?
[04:46] Janelle O: we saw spikes in 5xx for some in-flight requests as services timed out, but error budget impact was limited to a small percentage.
[04:55] Priya N: curious about the autoscaler heuristic - is it configuration we can tune?
[04:59] Ravi P: yes, autoscaler is policy-driven; we can tune thresholds, cooldowns, and add policy rules like "dont scale down below X replicas if 95th latency > Y".
[05:12] Laura K: and we also have options for pre-warm hooks - e.g. keep a small pool of warm workers for bursts or preload certain model KV prefix sets on scale-up.
[05:24] Markus L: pre-warm sounds useful. what's the cost tradeoff roughly?
[05:28] Laura K: small steady cost increase for the warm pool, but prevents cold-start tail spikes. we'll include a modeling spreadsheet for cost-vs-latency.
[05:40] Sofia R: on security/compliance - would the pre-warm process need additional access to keys or artifacts? we need to make sure it adheres to our KMS rules.
[05:49] Ravi P: pre-warm uses existing image artifacts and does not require exposing keys beyond what runtime already uses; for KV preload we may need read-only access to precomputed prefix bundles - we can provide a risk-mode that uses local ephemeral keys.
[06:05] Daniel O: want that in writing - any change that touches key handling must go to our compliance queue.
[06:10] Laura K: understood, we'll document flow and include a safe-mode option.
[06:18] [pause / crosstalk]
[06:25] Ravi P: medium term fixes we recommend: 1) tune autoscaler cooldown and min-replicas, 2) implement canary policy for scale-down, 3) improve KV eviction policy to favor hot prefixes, 4) better metrics instrumentation around cache-hit heatmaps.
[06:46] Priya N: for canary policy, do you mean tear down workers in smaller batches?
[06:50] Ravi P: yes, and only if latency metrics remain stable over a sliding window; essentially slow, measured scale-downs.
[07:00] Markus L: curious about instrumentation - can you add a heatmap that shows which prefixes are hottest so we can precompute?
[07:07] Ravi P: absolutely; we'll surface per-prefix hit rates and a recommended preload list.
[07:15] Janelle O: also adding a chaos test to your staging to simulate eviction storms might prevent recurrence - we can help set that up.
[07:25] Sofia R: agreed, and also would like an offline replay tool - we can replay traffic against a replica pool.
[07:32] Ravi P: we'll provide a replay harness; need sample traces from you.
[07:37] Markus L: timeline request - what does it look like for the soak test and subsequent config change?
[07:42] Laura K: propose: share sanitized traces by 6/18, repro in staging and run 48h soak 6/21-6/23, then review with you 6/24 and plan production rollout 6/28 if green.
[07:56] Priya N: that aligns with our internal calendar.
[08:02] Daniel O: one more security ask - confirm audit logs were persisted to your retention store and not truncated. in the incident window we need full fidelity.
[08:10] Ravi P: confirmed, we have full audit logs; retention policy can be adjusted per account. we'll include export instructions.
[08:20] [15 minutes of deeper tech discussion omitted here for brevity in transcript export but captured in deck]
[23:30] Sofia R: looking at autotune options, can you make autoscaler cooldown adjustable per route? some routes are more latency-sensitive than others.
[23:38] Ravi P: yes we have per-route policies; we can configure weighted cooldowns and route-level min replicas.
[23:45] Laura K: note - that is an enterprise feature in the Dedicated product; we'll include configuration examples.
[24:00] Markus L: how do we avoid cost surprises if we raise min replicas?
[24:05] Laura K: we can set a temporary budget cap for the soak test and alert you if usage approaches the cap. also provide an estimated cost delta in the spreadsheet.
[24:18] Priya N: do we have a recommended kv-ttl baseline?
[24:22] Ravi P: baseline depends on your workload; initial conservative change we suggested during incident was to bump ttl from 5m to 15m for affected prefixes, then tune down post-soak.
[24:35] Janelle O: note that longer TTL can increase memory pressure, so we need to balance with replica sizing.
[24:43] Sofia R: can you simulate memory pressure in staging?
[24:46] Ravi P: yes, we can add memory_poison test to the replay harness.
[24:52] Laura K: security note - if we preload KV bundles they should be stored encrypted and access audited; Ravi will provide implementation details.
[25:00] Daniel O: request captured.
[25:05] Markus L: any contractual stuff? we had mentioned SLA credits during the incident window.
[25:10] Laura K: we've already logged a support ticket for credit review; billing will follow up once the postmortem is finalized.
[25:20] Priya N: regarding the fallback to hosted variant, we'd like that to be opt-in; the automatic fallback is useful but we want control.
[25:28] Laura K: we can make routing fallbacks opt-in per-route and expose a flag in the console. we'll send instructions.
[25:37] [40 minutes mark - summary and actions]
[25:40] Laura K: ok recap - immediate items: sanitized logs & traces (Ravi + Sofia), postmortem deck (Redwood), pricing for temporary pool (Laura), staging replay (Priya + Redwood). medium term: autoscaler tuning, canary scale-down, preload lists, enhanced instrumentation.
[26:02] Markus L: thanks. can you confirm dates in email?
[26:05] Laura K: yes i'll follow up with meeting notes, deck, and the spreadsheet by Monday 6/14.
[26:12] Janelle O: assign owners in the doc so your internal teams can see responsibilities.
[26:18] Ravi P: one last technical add - we recommend adding a p99 proxy metric to the canary gating so you don't only rely on average.
[26:28] Sofia R: good call.
[26:33] Daniel O: security will review the pre-warm design; expect a follow-up question about key handling.
[26:40] Laura K: noted. anything else?
[26:43] [silence]
[26:45] Laura K: if not, thanks everyone. we'll circle on the next check-in after the soak test.
[26:50] Markus L: thanks all.
[26:52] [meeting end - 52:00 recorded length]
